text:
This page contains lecture notes, exercises, and supplementary material for Living in the IT Era, prepared primarily for the first-year BS Biology students whom I teach. The course is not intended to turn students into computer technicians or make them memorise catalogues of devices, inventors, and fashionable technologies. Its purpose is to provide enough working knowledge to make better decisions about computers, internet services, software, privacy, security, online conduct, AI, and other technologies that students encounter in ordinary life and scientific work.
Much of the subject will already be familiar in fragments. A student may know one part from using a phone, another from connecting to Wi-Fi, and another from hearing about online scams or AI. The course brings those pieces together, fills important gaps, and explains how they are related. Examples are drawn whenever practicable from biology, health, research, and Philippine digital life.
The eight-chapter plan is my working interpretation of the course’s assigned scope, adapted for biology students and current technological concerns. The notes will be developed as the course proceeds and may change in response to students’ questions, suggestions, and practical needs.

How classes will work
We shall use a flipped-classroom approach. Students first encounter the assigned material by reading the announced pages or sections before class. Class meetings will provide a bird’s-eye view of the chapter and concentrate on questions, discussion, examples, and practical applications rather than repeat the notes line by line.
The assigned reading will not usually be terribly long, and students are not expected to master it before class. They are, however, expected to read the assigned sections carefully rather than skim only the headings and examples. They should arrive familiar with the main ideas and ready to say what was clear, what was confusing, and what deserves further discussion. Reading before class is part of the course rather than optional preparation for it.

text: My hobby is independent mathematics, artificial intelligence, and machine-learning research. My current project asks a practical question: when an image is blurred, rotated, resized, poorly exposed, or corrupted by sensor noise, how does the information extracted by a computer change? I want to understand whether the pattern of those changes can help identify what went wrong during acquisition. This project continues the work begun in my University of Bristol final-year dissertation.
title: Hobby

text:
Retinal imaging and diabetic retinopathy
My interest in retinal imaging has a personal origin in an experience with diabetic retinopathy. It led me to take a particular interest in the reliability of retinal-image analysis.






Figure 1: An ordinary moment as children grow up. The second view represents one possible experience of sight loss associated with advanced diabetic retinopathy. The condition usually has no noticeable symptoms at first, and its later effects on vision vary. This is an explanatory illustration, not a clinical simulation. See the NHS overview of diabetic retinopathy.



The NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme offers a practical setting for this question. Fundus photographs are assessed against defined feature-based criteria within a structured grading and referral pathway. Trained graders inspect the images, uncertain or referable findings receive further review, and people who may need treatment are referred for clinical assessment.






Figure 2: A diabetic-retinopathy fundus image, annotated for my thesis to enlarge a connected lesion and examples of vascular loops. Source: image 214_D from the FIVES fundus-image dataset; reused and adapted under CC BY 4.0.



As the number of people requiring screening grows, so does the grading workload. Expanding trained grading capacity also takes time. The UK National Screening Committee recently consulted on automated retinal-image analysis as a possible way to triage images before human grading. At the time of the consultation, it did not recommend introducing automated grading into the programme. A conservative role for such systems is to support trained graders and clinical teams by handling suitable routine images and flagging abnormal, uncertain, or ungradable cases for human review. The research question is what mathematical and technical assurances would be needed before that assistance could be trusted at screening scale.
The same concern with reliability has a second practical direction: more informative quality checks and fault investigation in medical or industrial imaging systems. Some faults might eventually be assessed remotely before a specialist travels onsite. This is a direction for the research, not a capability of the present work.

How the project changed direction
My original intention was to produce a topology-informed classifier for diabetic retinopathy. Classifiers of this kind already existed, but reproducing and extending established work would still have been a useful objective for a four-month undergraduate project.
The direction changed during ablation testing, when I deliberately subjected the images to individual forms of degradation. A simulated rotation of roughly three degrees was enough to drive the selected topology-based classifier close to chance performance. That raised a practical question: what value would the classifier have if a slight change in the subject’s head alignment could cause it to fail? The topological vectors were highly sensitive to rotation and other mechanical changes that required the image to be resampled. Interpolation on the pixel grid could create or destroy topological features even when the underlying subject had changed very little. My undergraduate thesis described this behaviour as grid shattering.






Figure 3: A schematic DR-related vascular loop used to illustrate grid shattering. Above, alignment with the sampling grid preserves one cubical loop. Below, a small rotation followed by resampling fragments the pixel representation and destroys the detected loop, even though the underlying continuous vascular structure has not changed.



Once the ablation tests exposed this limitation, the project changed direction. Instead of treating the result as an inconvenience to the proposed classifier, I made it part of the research question and asked whether the contrasting failure behaviour could itself be useful.
In my thesis experiments, the same topological summaries were comparatively robust under several photometric changes, including exposure drift and quantisation, although not under every form of noise. Log-transformed Hu moments, which are geometric descriptors based on an image’s overall shape, showed a broadly reverse profile: they were comparatively strong under mechanical transformations but weaker under changes in intensity. Instead of asking either representation to serve as the classifier by itself, I treated them as two complementary, or “orthogonal”, controls.
I organised their contrasting failure profiles into what I called the Differential Failure Matrix. It was designed to test whether signatures associated with alignment and resampling could be distinguished from signatures associated with radiometric degradation. The final project was therefore not the classifier I had originally planned. It treated an apparent weakness of the cubical-persistence pipeline as a possible signal for a coarse fault-isolation heuristic. The code and supporting material are available in the project’s GitHub repository.


Questions left by the dissertation
The thesis was completed over four months. That was enough to establish and test the framework, but not to exhaust the questions it raised. The decomposition was descriptive and produced a suggestive empirical pattern, but it was mathematically coarse: its stability bound was conservative, and the final fault-isolation stage necessarily relied in part on empirical thresholds and heuristics. Time did not permit a deeper investigation of those mechanisms.
In a biomedical setting, a promising experimental result is not enough. The intended use, assumptions, limitations, performance, and possible failure modes of a method must be described and validated. My purpose in returning to the mathematics is to understand the underlying mechanisms more fully and to determine whether the heuristic parts of the pipeline can be replaced, constrained, or justified by stronger mathematical and empirical support. The longer-term aim is a pipeline whose assumptions and failure modes are more transparent and therefore easier to examine in technical and regulatory review. This is not a claim that the present work is a clinically validated or regulator-approved system.
Retinal imaging remains the immediate problem, and similar acquisition issues arise in industrial inspection and other computer-vision systems. My earlier experiments were confined to retinal images, so industrial applications remain a direction for further work.
title: Hobby

text:
Current focus
I am continuing to develop the mathematical foundations of this work, with a particular interest in making the system’s behaviour more explainable. Broadly, this means understanding why its components respond differently when an image changes, stating their assumptions and limitations more clearly, and improving how uncertainty and possible failures are communicated.
The work draws on topology, mathematical analysis, probability, and statistical machine learning. I am using these subjects to examine the pipeline from different angles rather than committing in advance to a particular theorem, model, or technical extension. The direction remains exploratory, and I will share further results when they are sufficiently developed.

The column appears in the Manila Bulletin every Saturday. The entries below link to individual columns; the newspaper also maintains an author archive.
View the Manila Bulletin archive


Who owns the future of work?
17 October 2026 · Manila Bulletin

AI may make workers more productive without making their livelihoods more secure. As machines take on more professional tasks, the gains could flow to those who own the technology while workers and smaller businesses pay for access. Education and retraining matter, but so do bargaining power, competitive technology markets, and opportunities to build assets alongside skills.
Read more



The Oracle of DelphAI
10 October 2026 · Manila Bulletin

What happens when AI supplies answers we can no longer judge for ourselves? Schools and workplaces may gain efficiency by automating difficult tasks, but those same tasks help beginners develop expertise. If we stop training people to think independently, dependence on imported intelligence could become as costly as dependence on imported oil.
Read more



AI seeks priests
3 October 2026 · Manila Bulletin

An AI that learns to improve itself may also get better at exploiting the gaps in our instructions. Who decides whether each change is an improvement, and who can stop it when it defeats the purpose of the rules? Effective oversight requires people and institutions capable of checking those claims and acting when safeguards fail.
Read more



When AI decides who is human
26 September 2026 · Manila Bulletin

An AI agent can follow an instruction while defeating the purpose behind it. Even a rule against harming people raises a difficult question: who does the system count as human? As we give machines more information and authority, the gaps between our intentions and their instructions become harder to dismiss as merely technical problems.
Read more



Can the world even afford an AI apocalypse?
19 September 2026 · Manila Bulletin

The lever is not merely unaffordable; under the present AI paradigm, it may not yet exist. Smaller models that run locally remain useful, and a new architecture may offer a better path. What remains doubtful is whether today’s large language models can become superintelligent simply by feeding them ever more chips, electricity, and capital.
Read more



Injecting more diskarte into the diploma
12 September 2026 · Manila Bulletin

Does entering adulthood really have to involve this much guesswork? We often say education prepares students for life. Perhaps that preparation can include practical matters such as opening a bank account, reading a payslip, dealing with government agencies, and starting a small business.
Read more



There’s something about Alex
5 September 2026 · Manila Bulletin

Alex(andra Eala) seems remarkably composed through all of it. She speaks carefully about representing the Philippines and about staying herself despite the attention. Frankly, I find that a little embarrassing. I did not have that kind of self-awareness at her age. I am not sure I had it even much later, when I already had an audience of my own.
Read more

This page contains lecture notes, examples, exercises, and supplementary material for Mathematics in the Modern World, prepared primarily for the BS Biology students whom I teach. This version of MMW combines mathematical appreciation with more calculation and reasoning than students may expect from a general-education course. It may feel challenging at times, but the work is intended to stretch students rather than overwhelm them. This emphasis follows the broad scope of Mathematics in the Modern World described in CHED Memorandum Order No. 20, series of 2013, while adapting the material to the needs of biology students.
The course has two aims. The first is to develop practical mathematical literacy—including financial literacy—that students can use in everyday life. The second is to introduce a little of several areas of mathematics in preparation for more advanced quantitative courses. Contrary to popular opinion, there is a great deal of mathematics in biology, so examples are drawn whenever possible from biology, ecology, health, and data analysis.
Biological and medical research is highly interdisciplinary. Students are not expected to master every field, but knowing something about different mathematical and computational approaches helps them recognise what a problem calls for—and whom they might ask to collaborate with, whether a statistician, mathematical modeller, computer scientist, or another specialist.
I think of this as a challenging but enjoyable course. Mathematics makes it possible to define terms clearly, state assumptions, and follow conclusions step by step. Its reputation, unfamiliar notation, or an earlier bad experience can make it appear less approachable than it is. Like any demanding subject, it becomes more manageable through careful study, practice, and learning from mistakes.

title: Discrete Structures for IT

text:
The Course
I will use this page to share course information, lecture notes, examples, exercises and supplementary material for our Discrete Structures for IT module at Bulacan State University’s Bustos Campus.
To be clear, this is a demanding first-year course in discrete mathematics. I expect everyone to engage deeply with the material. The keys to mastering mathematics are:

Practice, constant practice. Work through problems yourself and revisit the ones you find difficult.
Curiosity. Ask questions, even when they sound silly to you.
Diligence. Keep up with the material and work through your mistakes.

We will not be tackling Olympiad-level problems, and you do not need exceptional mathematical aptitude to do well. Think of this module as functional mathematical literacy for future IT specialists. We will work with logic, sets, functions, relations, counting, integers, induction, recursion, graphs and trees, connecting these ideas to organising records, expressing access rules and modelling networks.
This course prioritises depth over breadth. We will focus on selected topics and spend enough time on explanation, practice and feedback for you to become confident in using them. The aim is to develop lasting mathematical skills, rather than rush through a long list of topics that you only partly understand.
If you want to learn how to wrangle information, mathematics will give you the tools to do it precisely and systematically.
BulSU aims to be a globally competitive university, and I want you to take pride in your studies. Drawing on my experience at Bristol, I will expect the same independent study, careful reasoning and active participation that I encountered as a student there.
title: Discrete Structures for IT

Primary textbook
Oscar Levin’s Discrete Mathematics: An Open Introduction, fourth edition, is our primary textbook. You can read it online or download the PDF for free. We will use selected sections, with supplementary examples where needed.

text:
Tentative course outline
The thirteen teaching weeks follow Levin’s progression through logic and proofs, graphs, counting, sequences, and sets and functions. Each chapter in our lecture notes corresponds to one teaching week; these chapter numbers are separate from Levin’s. We will study selected material within the sections listed below.








Ch.
Topics
Levin, fourth edition




1
Mathematical statements, predicates and quantifiers
§1.1; definitions from §0.2 as needed


2
Implications, logical equivalence and valid arguments
§§1.2–1.3


3
Direct proof, contrapositive and contradiction
§1.4


4
Proofs about sets, functions and relations
§§1.5.2–1.5.4


5
Graphs and trees
§§2.1–2.2


6
Relations, their properties, equivalence classes and partitions
§2.6


7
Counting outcomes: sum and product rules, inclusion–exclusion
§§3.1–3.3


8
Combinations, permutations and combinatorial proofs
§§3.4 and 3.6


9
Sequences: explicit and recursive descriptions, initial conditions, arithmetic and geometric sequences
§§4.1–4.2


10
Ordinary (weak) mathematical induction
§4.5


11
Strong induction
§4.6


12
Sets and functions revisited: operations, function properties and recursive definitions
§§5.1–5.2


13
Structural induction on recursively defined objects, including expressions and rooted trees
Supplementary material drawing on earlier topics



There will be no coding assignments, but pseudocode may be used to explain mathematical ideas and algorithms. Recursive functions will be studied through their domains, initial values, defining rules and mathematical evaluation. Structural induction will receive a supplementary explanation and exercises.

NoteRespect for learning



There is room for humour in this class—you can even joke about me, and I will happily laugh along. But please take the subject seriously. Making a mistake or struggling to understand is part of learning; treating a lack of understanding as something to celebrate is another matter. Take pride in your studies, respect the effort your classmates put into learning, and give the course content the attention it deserves.



Electronic devices: Phones and other personal electronic devices must be switched off and put away during class. Approved accessibility arrangements and university-required exceptions take precedence.
Photo: Please bring a recent 1×1 photo to our first class so I can identify you when recording attendance.
Seating: We will use a fixed seating plan to help me record attendance and class recitation.
Attention and classroom conduct: We meet only once a week for three hours, so each session can be more demanding than shorter classes spread across the week. I expect everyone to listen carefully and stay focused, even when the material gets difficult. If you are struggling to follow, please interrupt me and ask, or raise your questions during consultations. Disruptive chatting, excessive noise, and other misbehaviour are unacceptable and will be addressed through the university’s prescribed disciplinary procedures. Participation marks follow the approved assessment criteria. I am preparing you for life beyond university, where discipline matters.
Coursework and deadlines: Submit coursework by the stated deadline. Work not submitted by the deadline receives zero marks, unless an excused absence or another university-approved arrangement applies. An unexcused absence does not extend a deadline or entitle you to a make-up assessment. Work submitted on time is assessed under the published criteria.
Attendance and punctuality: Attend regularly and arrive on time. Under the handbook, arrival 15 minutes after the scheduled start is recorded as tardy, and arrival 20 minutes after the start is recorded as absent. Being marked absent does not prevent you from attending the lesson. Unexcused absences exceeding 20% of required class time before midterms trigger automatic dropping, recorded as FDA (failure due to absences) or UD (unofficially dropped). My course policy allows a maximum of three unexcused absences, subject to university attendance rules. Given the pace of this course, I strongly recommend perfect attendance. The official attendance calculation uses the required semester contact hours, and the count does not reset after midterms. Attendance classifications and grades follow university rules; FDA/UD and a numerical grade of 5.0 are distinct classifications.
Missed examinations: If you miss an examination for an excused reason, contact me promptly with supporting documentation. Special examinations require the instructor’s recommendation and the unit head’s approval under Part II, Section J. Your final examination is not automatically double-weighted. An unexcused missed examination receives zero marks under the course assessment arrangements, subject to applicable university policies.
Excused absences: The handbook recognises official university representation, medically certified sickness, and force majeure as excused reasons. Notify me promptly and provide the relevant documentation. An excused absence does not waive coursework requirements; arrange to complete any missed work. The handbook also sets a 30% limit on excused absences.
Assessment and concerns: Assessment components, weights, and marking criteria follow the approved syllabus. You may ask how your marks were calculated and request a review of your class standing. Raise concerns with me or use the university’s student grievance procedure.
Borderline marks: I may extend consideration to students with borderline failing marks who have perfect attendance, where permitted by the approved assessment rules. This is discretionary and does not guarantee a passing grade or waive academic requirements.
Use of AI: I strongly encourage you to use AI for revision, but not to solve your problem sets. If AI does the work for you, you are likely to fail the midterm and final examinations, which use zero-based grading.

Course-specific arrangements and updates will be communicated through official class channels.

About me
I graduated with a BSc in Mathematics with first-class honours from the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom. My interests lie in applying probability, topological data analysis, artificial intelligence and machine learning, network science, and combinatorics to problems in healthcare, industry, and public policy.
In the previous semester, I taught Mathematics in the Modern World and Living in the IT Era at Bulacan State University’s San Rafael Campus. Before that, I was a teaching assistant for Mathematical Programming at the University of Bristol.
During weekdays, I serve as an Assistant Secretary at the Office of the Cabinet Secretary in the Office of the President, Government of the Philippines. My work includes policy analytics, where I use mathematical methods, among other tools, to assess the feasibility and reasonableness of proposed and existing government policies. On Saturdays, I teach you. On Sundays, I study for my MSc in Applied and Computational Mathematics at The Johns Hopkins University in the United States. In what little spare time I have, I catch Pokémon.

You can call me RJ, Kuya RJ, or Sir—though “Sir” sounds a little icky because I have not been knighted by King Charles. Call me Tito RJ or Daddy RJ and I will automatically fail you. But seriously, just call me RJ (no honorifics), and that’s totally fine.
